analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder and costlier for individuals to erase debts in bankruptcy and pushes more into repayment plans.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 88 cosponsors, the House bill never reached a floor vote; an identically named Senate bill became law in April 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal bankruptcy law to push more individual debtors out of Chapter 7, which wipes out most debts, and into Chapter 13 repayment plans, using a formula (the 'means test') built on IRS expense standards. Everyone filing would first have to complete paid credit counseling, bankruptcy attorneys would face personal liability for their clients' filings, the wait between discharges would lengthen, and people with income above their state median would face a presumption that filing is 'abuse.' The bill also carries real protections: child support claims get first priority, retirement and education savings are shielded, borrowers get new disclosures on reaffirmation agreements and predatory loans, and family farmers and fishermen get permanent bankruptcy protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card issuers, banks, and other lenders gain the most: the means test routes more debtors into plans where creditors are repaid rather than discharged, and secured lenders get faster relief from bankruptcy's automatic stay. Credit counseling agencies gain a mandatory customer base, since no one can file without one. Families owed child support, retirement savers, and borrowers holding predatory loans gain specific new protections.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a 'means test' that presumes abuse for debtors whose income, after IRS-standard expenses, exceeds thresholds, pushing them into Chapter 13 repayment plans instead of Chapter 7 debt erasure.
Requires every individual debtor to receive credit counseling from an approved nonprofit agency within 180 days before filing, and to complete a financial management course before discharge.
Gives domestic support obligations — child support and alimony — first priority over most other claims and makes them largely nondischargeable.
Protects retirement savings and education savings from being counted as assets available to creditors in bankruptcy.
Preserves a borrower's claims and defenses against predatory loans when the loan is sold to a third party, and imposes a standardized disclosure form for debt reaffirmation agreements.
Permanently reenacts Chapter 12 bankruptcy protection for family farmers and extends it to family fishermen.
Adds protections for patients of insolvent health care businesses, including an ombudsman to act as patient advocate, and raises the priority of employee wages and benefits in business bankruptcies.
Requires new credit card disclosures covering introductory rates, late-payment deadlines, and penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Households in financial distress pay more to seek relief — counseling fees, attorney fees pushed up by new lawyer-liability rules, and, for many, three to five years of repayment instead of a fresh start. People with modest incomes above their state median bear the brunt of the means test.

drawbacks.text: The means test calculates allowable living expenses from fixed IRS schedules rather than a family's actual costs, so debtors with incomes above their state median can be presumed abusive even when real expenses absorb their income.
Mandatory pre-filing credit counseling adds a fee and a delay before relief, applying to every filer, including those below median income whom the means test never targets.

Bankruptcy attorneys must certify under penalty that they investigated each filing, and courts can order them to pay trustees' costs for motions they lose, raising the price of representation for debtors.
Chapter 13 plans would run five years in certain cases, and the waiting period between bankruptcy discharges would be extended, keeping debtors under court supervision longer.
New restrictions on 'debt relief agencies' — the lawyers and services that advise debtors — limit the advice they can give and add disclosure requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles a handful of genuine debtor protections — child support priority, retirement and education savings shields, predatory-loon and reaffirmation disclosures, farm and fisherman bankruptcy access — around a core that shifts leverage decisively toward creditors. The consumer-protection title is largely disclosures, while the operative change is that far fewer households can erase their debts. The IRS-standard means test is rigid by design: it replaces a judge's look at real circumstances with a formula, and later experience showed most filers were pushed there by job loss, medical bills, or divorce rather than the serial abuse the bill targeted. An honest supporter could defend the anti-abuse goal; the honest cost is that struggling working families pay for it.

outcome.mechanism: The House bill never came to a vote: it sat in the Judiciary and Financial Services committees and their subcommittees from February 2005 until the Congress ended, while the Senate moved its own identically named companion bill, which President Bush signed into law in April 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 9, 2005, and referred to both the Judiciary Committee and the Financial Services Committee.

By mid-May 2005 it had been referred to two subcommittees — Commercial and Administrative Law, and Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit — and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 109th Congress.
It carried 88 cosponsors at introduction: 80 Republicans and 8 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, banks, and other consumer lenders are better off, because the substance of this bill became law anyway through the Senate companion in April 2005. Households in financial distress are worse off, facing a means test, mandatory counseling, and longer repayment before they can clear their debts.

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up an initial cross-party list of 60-plus original cosponsors.

for.name: House cosponsors (80 Republicans, 8 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill a broad early base of support.

for.name: Senate majority (109th Congress)
for.role: Senate passers of the companion bill
for.what_they_did: Passed the identically named Senate companion (S. 256) in March 2005, which became the vehicle that enacted the policy.

for.name: Consumer credit card and banking industry
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for over a decade for a means test and tighter bankruptcy rules, making this the industry's top legislative priority.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the Senate companion version of the bill into law in April 2005.

against.name: Consumer advocacy groups and consumer bankruptcy attorneys
against.what_they_did: Argued the bill would deny debt relief to families hit by job loss, medical bills, and divorce while the targeted 'abusers' were rare.

against.name: House Democratic opponents
against.what_they_did: Most House Democrats did not cosponsor and opposed the bill's core means-test and creditor provisions in the broader debate.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was 80 Republicans to 8 Democrats, and the broader fight over the identical Senate bill split largely on party lines, though final passage of that companion drew some bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The means test, longer discharge gaps, and curbs on repeat filings route more debtors into plans where lenders are repaid instead of debts being erased. The industry pursued this change for about a decade as its leading legislative goal.

Mandatory pre-filing counseling makes approved agencies a required, fee-charging stop before every bankruptcy filing, whether or not counseling helps. The bill creates the rules that keep them in that gatekeeping role.

The bill speeds relief from the automatic stay when debtors fail to surrender collateral and strengthens secured creditors' position in Chapter 13, so lenders recover collateral faster and collect more.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy attorneys and debt relief agencies
industries.note: Lawyer-liability certifications, fee exposure for lost motions, and new restrictions on advice raise the cost and risk of representing debtors. Their interest in opposing runs alongside debtors' interest in affordable relief.

The bill permanently reenacts Chapter 12 debt adjustment for family farmers and extends it to family fishermen, a durable protection for small agricultural operators. This gain sits alongside the bill's broader creditor-friendly tilt.
